newsitem.title: USA: UPS, union resume talks ahead of strike deadline.
newsitem.headline: UPS, union resume talks ahead of strike deadline.

text.p: The International Brotherhood of Teamsters and United Parcel Service, the biggest U.S. parcel carrier, resumed contract talks on Sunday evening in a last-ditch bid to avert a potentially crippling strike.
Teamsters President Ron Carey repeated the union's threat to walk out after a midnight EDT deadline (0400 GMT on Monday GMT) if no new contract had been agreed upon.
"If the company does not address the issues ... I assure you at 12:01, we'll be on strike," Carey said as his delegation arrived for the talks around 7:30 p.m. EDT (2330 GMT).

Carey held out the hope that the two parties would be able to reach agreement with the help of a federal mediator, but union officials said there were still significant disagreements on several key issues when they last met.

"I don't have a crystal ball, but I've always said ... that I'm optimistic," Carey said, noting the company had not yet responded to a comprehensive proposal submitted by the union to the federal mediator on Saturday evening.
UPS Chairman and CEO James Kelly and his negotiating team arrived about an hour before the union to meet with the mediator and consider the union proposal.

"We are willing and ready to continue talking with the Teamsters this evening," said UPS spokeswoman Gina Ellrich, noting that the threat of a strike had already reduced the carrier's shipping volume by one million packages from 12 million, forcing it to lay off several thousand workers.
"We are working hard to resolve the issues together," she said.
A White House spokesman said the Clinton administration was keeping a close eye on the talks, and the president was hopeful a strike would be averted.
"We hope that the talks will continue and that negotiators will work out an agreement," said spokesman Barry Toiv. "We are continuing to monitor the situtation."
Carey said the union was particularly concerned about preventing work going to subcontractors rather than union workers, the pension plan, and health and safety issues.
Union spokesman Rand Wilson said the two sides were "still pretty far apart on all the issues", including whether the contract would last for three, four or five years.
"It's time for UPS to choose between a strike and a contract that provides good jobs and pensions," Carey said.
But Ellrich said UPS had offered to give 10,000 part-time workers full-time jobs over the life of the contract, adding that UPS workers had the best-paying jobs in the industry.

Union officials were taking a firm stand against what they call a continuing effort by UPS to shift full-time work to part-time positions. Some 60 percent of all UPS workers are now on part-time status, far above the national average of 18 percent as well as part-time rates at the U.S. Postal Service.
Wilson also noted that the company had agreed only to create 200 new full-time jobs, with the rest of the 10,000 positions to be filled as drivers retired or quit.

Wells said a strike would adversely affect "a lot" of Americans. Atlanta-based UPS employs 301,000 people in the United States, 185,000 of whom are represented by the Teamsters, including package sorters, loaders and drivers.
UPS said last week that the threat of a strike was costing it about $5 million a day in business lost to competitors such as the Postal Service and Federal Express Corp.

In what it called its "last, best and final" contract offer on Thursday, the company offered to boost pay for both full- and part-time workers by $1.50 to $2.50 per hour over five years. Under the company proposal, a profit-sharing plan would provide a first payment of $3,060 to full-time employees and $1,530 to part-time workers in 1997.
With revenue of $22.4 billion in 1996, UPS annually handles about three billion parcels and documents, shipped to more than 200 countries from 1,700 hubs and centres.
